passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The people pray for their king before a battle. “May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you” (verse 1). “May He send you help from the sanctuary and sustain you from Zion” (verse 2). “May He give you the desires of your heart and make all your plans succeed” (verse 4).

Then one voice speaks with sudden confidence: “Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed” (verse 6).

The heart of the psalm is this: “Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (verse 7). The psalm ends with a short cry: “O LORD, save the king. Answer us on the day we call” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This is a royal psalm, a prayer for the king of David's line as he went out to war. The people speak to the king in verses 1 to 5. The king, or a priest or prophet, answers in verse 6. Many scholars think it was used in the temple before battle, with offerings (verse 3).

Chariots were the strongest weapon of the ancient world. Egypt and the Canaanite cities had them; Israel in the hill country had few for much of its history. Its story began with Pharaoh's chariots sunk in the sea (Exodus 15:4). So ‘some trust in chariots’ was not a general saying. It named the power that every nation counted on, and set God's name against it.

‘The name’ appears three times in nine verses. In the Bible a name means who someone has shown himself to be.
passages.later:
The prophets kept saying the same thing to kings who forgot it. “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses, who trust in their abundance of chariots” (Isaiah 31:1). Proverbs puts it simply: “A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31). Young David told Goliath, “I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts” (1 Samuel 17:45).

The New Testament does not quote this psalm. Christians read its prayer for ‘His anointed’ in the light of Jesus, the anointed King whom God answered by raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand (Acts 2:33).
passages.hard: Is this a prayer for any nation's army? No. It was a prayer for Israel's king, the anointed of David's line, under God's covenant. No modern nation stands in that place, and the book page says so in its part on the royal psalms. The psalm's own lesson cuts the other way: it warns every nation against trusting its own strength.
passages.asks:
What are your chariots? Money, health, skill, a plan, people who owe you? None of them is evil. The psalm asks what you trust when the day of trouble comes.

It also teaches you to pray for leaders, by name, before their hard days.
